prompt_version: s5-extract-facts-v2 (adapted from Paleo Atlas extract-facts-v3; v2 after Sofía's S5 review)

facts.statement: The study was a retrospective cross-sectional analysis of 74 patients who had not yet received treatment and 91 healthy controls.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Researchers compared blood test results for inflammation and blood cell counts between people experiencing their first episode of psychosis or mania and healthy individuals.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The patient group showed higher levels of white blood cells, neutrophils, and platelets, along with several calculated inflammation scores, while having lower values for platelet size distribution and volume ratios.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: There were no significant differences in the measured inflammatory markers between the group with first-episode psychosis and the group with a first manic episode.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: After adjusting for age, sex, and body mass index, white blood cell count, neutrophil count, and three specific inflammation indices were statistically associated with being in the patient group.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The three complex inflammation indices did not add any significant explanatory power beyond what was already provided by the neutrophil count alone.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The findings suggest that signs of immune system activation in the blood may be present in the early stages of these psychiatric conditions before treatment begins.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Because the two patient groups showed similar inflammatory profiles, these blood markers are limited in their ability to distinguish between psychosis and mania for diagnostic purposes.
facts.subject: humans
